title: Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor
hook: A flute leads a small string band through a chain of French dances, and ends with a quick joke, the Badinerie.

painting.title: Concert Champêtre
painting.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
painting.pairingNote: A music party in a park in the 1730s, a young man playing a pipe and a woman a hurdy-gurdy; the French taste for elegant country pleasures that Bach’s suite of French dances, led by a flute, carried to Leipzig.

facts: Bach wrote four orchestral suites, which he called *ouvertures* after their long opening movements; they were not planned as a set. This one survives in a set of parts from Leipzig dated 1738–39, and Bach wrote out the flute and viola parts himself. It is the latest of the four. In October 1739 he went back to directing the Collegium Musicum, the society that gave weekly concerts at Zimmermann’s coffee house, and the suite may well have been played there.

It is the only one of the four with a solo instrument: a transverse flute that plays almost all the time, so the suite is close to a flute concerto disguised as a set of French dances. The rest of the band is just strings and [[continuo|continuo]].

The flute may not have been the first idea. The scholar Joshua Rifkin has argued, from mistakes in the surviving parts, that they were copied from an earlier version a tone lower, in A minor, for solo violin; at the top of the solo part Bach seems to have turned a “V” into the “T” of “Traversiere”. Others think the original soloist was an oboe. The question is open.

The dances are French, apart from the Polonaise, which is based on a Polish folk song. Bach’s own sovereign, the Elector of Saxony, was also King of Poland, and in 1736 Bach received the title of court composer to him. The last movement, the Badinerie (“jest”; Bach spelled it “Battinerie”), has become one of the best-known showpieces for the flute.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a grand French overture (I), five dances, from graceful to stately (II–VI), and a quick, playful finale for the flute (VII).

movements.heading: Ouverture
movements.title: Ouverture
movements.summary: A [[french-overture|French overture]] in three parts: a slow, stately opening in jerky dotted rhythms, a fast middle section that starts like a [[fugue|fugue]], and a slow close. In the fast section the flute keeps stepping out of the band for solo passages, as in a concerto.

mainIdeas.name: The slow music
mainIdeas.description: heavy, solemn chords in a long-short dotted rhythm, with the flute doubling the first violins.

mainIdeas.name: The fast theme
mainIdeas.description: a busy line taken up by one part after another.

mainIdeas.name: The flute’s solos
mainIdeas.description: quick, light passages over a thinner accompaniment.

stops.hear: Slow, solemn chords in a jerky long-short rhythm; the flute is blended into the violins
stops.happening: The slow opening of the [[french-overture|French overture]], in B minor

stops.hear: The same solemn opening again
Suddenly quicker: a busy theme starts in one part and the others enter one after another
The flute steps forward alone with quick, light passages; the full band answers between them
stops.happening: Solo episodes, like a concerto inside the overture

stops.hear: The music slows again into a grave, swaying three-time

notice: In the fast section, listen for the moments when the band thins out and the flute is heard on its own. They are the concerto inside the suite.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The English Concert play on period instruments, with Stephen Preston on a wooden Baroque flute, softer and more veiled than a modern metal one, and Trevor Pinnock directing from the harpsichord. In the overture they repeat only the slow opening section. On the Spotify album the suite is tracks 1–7, followed by Suite No. 3.

movements.heading: Rondeau
movements.title: Rondeau
movements.summary: A graceful dance in the rhythm of a gavotte, each phrase starting in the middle of the bar. As in any [[rondo|rondo]], a short refrain keeps coming back between two contrasting passages.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a poised, gently lilting tune in the flute and first violins.

stops.hear: A poised, lilting tune in flute and violins, played twice
A new phrase that wanders away from the home key
The lilting tune again
A longer, more searching passage

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The tune one last time

notice: Count how many times the opening tune returns. It frames everything else in the movement.

movements.heading: Sarabande
movements.title: Sarabande
movements.summary: A slow, dignified [[sarabande|sarabande]], with the weight on the second beat of the bar. Under the calm surface Bach hides a puzzle: the bass plays the same melody as the flute and first violins, a little later and much lower, so the movement is a [[canon|canon]].

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: slow and noble, in the flute with the first violins.

mainIdeas.name: The bass
mainIdeas.description: the same melody again, starting a moment later and an octave and a fifth lower.

stops.hear: A slow, noble melody on top; after a moment the bass begins the same melody deep below
stops.happening: A [[canon|canon]] between the top line and the bass

stops.hear: The first half again
The second half, moving through other keys, the bass still following the melody
The second half repeated, ending quietly in B minor

notice: Listen to the lowest instruments. They are not simply supporting the tune; they are singing it too, a little behind.

movements.heading: Bourrée I–II
movements.title: Bourrée I–II
movements.summary: Two quick French dances in two, played one after the other, then the first comes back. In the second bourrée the flute takes the spotlight with a running line.

mainIdeas.name: Bourrée I
mainIdeas.description: brisk and lively, for the whole band, with a short upbeat into each phrase.

mainIdeas.name: Bourrée II
mainIdeas.description: lighter, the flute running over a quieter accompaniment.

stops.hear: A brisk, bouncing dance for everyone
Lighter; the flute runs above the strings
The brisk first dance again, this time without repeats

notice: Compare the two bourrées. The first is for the band; the second is a small feature for the flute.

movements.heading: Polonaise – Double
movements.title: Polonaise – Double
movements.summary: A stately Polish dance in three, built on a folk song. In the middle comes the Double, a variation: the tune moves down into the bass, and above it the flute plays a decorated line. Then the Polonaise returns.

mainIdeas.name: The Polonaise
mainIdeas.description: a proud, stately tune with a dotted rhythm, in flute and violins.

mainIdeas.name: The Double
mainIdeas.description: the same tune in the bass instruments, with a flowing flute line above and almost nothing else.

stops.hear: A proud, stately tune in three, with a snapping dotted rhythm
The texture thins to two lines: the tune deep in the bass, the flute weaving quick decorations above
stops.happening: The Double, a variation with the melody in the bass

stops.hear: The stately tune for the full band again

notice: In the Double, follow the bass line. It is the Polonaise tune you heard at the start, now at the bottom of the music.

movements.heading: Menuet
movements.title: Menuet
movements.summary: A short, simple [[minuet|minuet]] in three, in two halves, each played twice. Its calm is the pause before the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The minuet tune
mainIdeas.description: plain and graceful, in flute and violins, over a steady bass.

stops.hear: A plain, graceful tune in three
The same phrase again
The second half, longer, moving away and back
The second half again

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A quiet close in B minor

notice: Notice how short and plain this movement is after the Polonaise. It clears the air for the Badinerie.

movements.heading: Badinerie
movements.title: Badinerie
movements.summary: The finale is a jest: a very fast, playful dance in two in which the flute hardly stops for breath. It is in two halves, each played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The Badinerie tune
mainIdeas.description: a quick, leaping figure in the flute that falls down a broken chord and bounces back.

stops.hear: A fast, leaping flute tune over crisp strings
stops.happening: The first half of the Badinerie

stops.hear: The first half again
The second half: the tune turns and travels through other keys, the flute still racing
The second half again, to the end
stops.happening: The repeat and a quick, light close

notice: Listen for where the flautist can breathe. In the fastest passages there is almost no room.

threads.title: A concerto in disguise
threads.body: The flute takes solos in the overture, gets its own bourrée and the decorations of the Double, and carries the finale alone.

threads.title: France in Leipzig
threads.body: A French overture and French dances, written in Saxony for German players, with a Polish dance in the middle for good measure.

threads.title: One key throughout
threads.body: Every movement is in B minor. The variety comes from the dances’ rhythms and from what the flute is doing, not from changes of key.
